(1) The use of a liquid stationary film in gas chromatography is one of the best choices for the separation of complex mixtures of compounds, especially if the separation of the compounds is based on the differences in their boiling points.
The use of a liquid stationary phases is one of the main advantages of gas chromatography.

the development and application of gas chromatography to the analysis of organic compounds in the gas phase and in solution.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the choice of a liquid stationary for a particular separation should be based on the results of a series of experiments using test mixtures and that the best results are obtained with a liquid phase which is as non-polar as possible and as selective as necessary to achieve the required separation.
the choice of an appropriate liquid phase for a given separation problem is a matter of trial and error.

the most suitable liquid for a particular separation is that one which provides the greatest separation factor for the components to be separated and which has the lowest retention value for the most strongly retained component.

the use of liquid phases for gas chromatographic separations should be restricted to those compounds which are not thermally stable or are too volatile for the use of solid phases.
the use of a liquid phase with a low boiling point, high volatility and low viscosity is advantageous, especially in open tubular columns.

liquid stationary phases are a valuable tool for the gas chromatographer and that the use of the Rohrschneider constants is a useful tool for the selection of a stationary phase for a specific separation.

the choice of stationary phase is a very important decision to be made when designing a GC method.
